blocks.body:
Pick up a square and put it back so that it covers exactly the same region. There are eight ways to do it: four rotations (by $0^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$, $270^\circ$) and four reflections (in the two diagonals and in the two lines joining midpoints of opposite sides). Doing one of these motions and then another is again one of them, each can be undone, and doing nothing is one of them. A group is what remains when you keep these three features and forget the square.

The reward for abstracting is that one argument then covers rotations, permutations, numbers modulo $n$ and invertible matrices at once. This page builds the definition and proves the first two tools: Lagrange's theorem (the size of a subgroup of a finite group divides the size of the group, which contains Fermat's little theorem as a special case) and Burnside's lemma (a formula for counting objects up to symmetry, such as colourings of a cube).

blocks.title: Symmetries compose, and order matters
blocks.body:
Number the corners of the square $1,2,3,4$ going anticlockwise. A symmetry moves corners to corners, so it can be recorded as a permutation of $\{1,2,3,4\}$. Let $r$ be the anticlockwise rotation by $90^\circ$, so $r$ sends $1\to2\to3\to4\to1$, and let $s$ be the reflection in the diagonal through corners $1$ and $3$, so $s$ fixes $1$ and $3$ and swaps $2$ and $4$.

Write $rs$ for "first do $s$, then do $r$" (the usual convention for composing functions). Then $rs$ sends corner $1$ to $r(s(1)) = r(1) = 2$, while $sr$ sends $1$ to $s(r(1)) = s(2) = 4$. So $rs \ne sr$: working out all four corners, $rs$ swaps $1\leftrightarrow2$ and $3\leftrightarrow4$ (a reflection in a line through edge midpoints), while $sr$ swaps $1\leftrightarrow4$ and $2\leftrightarrow3$ (the other such reflection).

Three facts are visible already. Composition of symmetries is associative, because composition of functions always is. There is an identity motion. Every motion has an inverse. Commutativity, on the other hand, fails, and the theory has to live without it.

blocks.title: Group
Examples, non-examples and first consequences
blocks.body:
Examples to keep in mind:

- $(\mathbb Z, +)$: the identity is $0$ and the inverse of $a$ is $-a$. Abelian and infinite.
- $\mathbb Z/n$, the residues $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ under addition modulo $n$ ([[congruences]]). Abelian, order $n$.
- $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$ for a prime $p$: the nonzero residues $1, \dots, p-1$ under multiplication modulo $p$. Inverses exist because every $a$ with $p \nmid a$ has a [[mod-inverse|modular inverse]]. Order $p-1$. More generally $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$, the residues coprime to $n$, is a group of order $\varphi(n)$ ([[arithmetic-functions]]).
- $S_n$, all permutations of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ under composition. Order $n!$; not abelian once $n \ge 3$.
- $D_n$, the symmetries of a regular $n$-gon: $n$ rotations and $n$ reflections, order $2n$. The square group above is $D_4$.
- The invertible $2\times 2$ real matrices under matrix multiplication.

Non-examples: $(\mathbb N, +)$ has no inverses; the integers under multiplication have no inverse for $2$; and $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$ under multiplication modulo $6$ is not even closed, since $2 \cdot 3 \equiv 0 \pmod 6$.

A few rules follow at once from the axioms. The identity is unique: if $e$ and $e'$ both work then $e = ee' = e'$. Inverses are unique, and we may cancel: if $ab = ac$ then multiplying on the left by $a^{-1}$ gives $b = c$. Also $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$ (undo the last action first), since $(ab)(b^{-1}a^{-1}) = a(bb^{-1})a^{-1} = e$. Powers are defined as usual: $g^0 = e$, $g^{n+1} = g^n g$, and $g^{-n} = (g^{-1})^n$.

blocks.title: Subgroup and order of an element
blocks.body:
A subset $H \subseteq G$ is a subgroup if it contains $e$ and is closed under the operation and under taking inverses; $H$ is then a group in its own right. The order $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ of an element $g$ is the least $n \ge 1$ with $g^n = e$, if such an $n$ exists.

If $\operatorname{ord}(g) = n$, the powers $e, g, \dots, g^{n-1}$ are distinct (if $g^i = g^j$ with $0 \le i < j < n$ then $g^{j-i} = e$ with $0 < j-i < n$), and they form a subgroup $\langle g \rangle$ with exactly $n$ elements, since $g^n = e$ makes the powers wrap around and $g^{n-i}$ is the inverse of $g^i$. In a finite group every element has finite order, because the powers of $g$ cannot all be different.

blocks.title: Cosets: slicing a group into equal pieces
blocks.body:
Take $G = \mathbb Z/12$ (written additively) and the subgroup $H = \{0, 4, 8\}$. Shifting $H$ by each element gives only four different sets:

$$\{0,4,8\},\quad \{1,5,9\},\quad \{2,6,10\},\quad \{3,7,11\}.$$

They do not overlap, they cover $G$, and each has $3$ elements, so $12 = 4 \cdot 3$. That is Lagrange's theorem in miniature.

In general, for a subgroup $H$ of $G$ and an element $g$, the left coset of $H$ through $g$ is $gH = \{gh : h \in H\}$. In additive notation it is $g + H$.

blocks.title: Lagrange's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $H$ a subgroup. Then the distinct left cosets of $H$ partition $G$ and each has exactly $|H|$ elements. Hence

$$|G| = [G:H]\cdot|H|,$$

where the index $[G:H]$ is the number of left cosets. In particular $|H|$ divides $|G|$.

We check three facts.

1. Every $g \in G$ lies in some coset, namely $g = ge \in gH$.
2. Every coset has $|H|$ elements: the map $h \mapsto gh$ from $H$ to $gH$ is onto by the definition of $gH$, and one-to-one by cancellation ($gh_1 = gh_2$ implies $h_1 = h_2$).
3. Two cosets are either equal or disjoint. Suppose $x \in aH \cap bH$, say $x = ah_1 = bh_2$ with $h_1, h_2 \in H$. Then $a = bh_2h_1^{-1}$, so for every $h \in H$ we get $ah = b(h_2h_1^{-1}h)$, which lies in $bH$ because $H$ is closed under products and inverses. Thus $aH \subseteq bH$, and the same argument with $a$ and $b$ exchanged gives $bH \subseteq aH$.

So the distinct cosets cut $G$ into $[G:H]$ disjoint blocks of size $|H|$, and $|G| = [G:H]\,|H|$.
blocks.title: Proof of Lagrange's theorem
Consequences of Lagrange
blocks.body:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $g \in G$. Then $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ divides $|G|$, and $g^{|G|} = e$.

Taking $G = (\mathbb Z/p)^\times$ gives Fermat's little theorem: $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ whenever $p \nmid a$. Taking $G = (\mathbb Z/n)^\times$ gives Euler's theorem: $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ whenever $\gcd(a,n) = 1$.

The cyclic subgroup $\langle g \rangle$ has $\operatorname{ord}(g)$ elements, so by Lagrange $|G| = k \cdot \operatorname{ord}(g)$ for some integer $k$. Then $g^{|G|} = \big(g^{\operatorname{ord}(g)}\big)^k = e^k = e$. The two congruences are this statement read inside the groups $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$, of order $p-1$, and $(\mathbb Z/n)^\times$, of order $\varphi(n)$.

blocks.title: Groups acting on sets
blocks.body:
Groups usually arrive as symmetries of something: of a square, of the set of colourings of a necklace, of the roots of a polynomial. The general notion is an action.

An action of a group $G$ on a set $X$ assigns to each $g \in G$ and $x \in X$ an element $g\cdot x \in X$ such that $e \cdot x = x$ and $g\cdot(h\cdot x) = (gh)\cdot x$ for all $g, h, x$. For $x \in X$ and $g \in G$ define

- the orbit $\operatorname{Orb}(x) = \{g\cdot x : g \in G\}$, everywhere $x$ can be moved to;
- the stabiliser $\operatorname{Stab}(x) = \{g \in G : g\cdot x = x\}$, a subgroup of $G$;
- the fixed set $\operatorname{Fix}(g) = \{x \in X : g\cdot x = x\}$.

Two points are in the same orbit exactly when some group element moves one to the other; this is an equivalence relation (use $e$, inverses and composition), so the orbits partition $X$.

For the square group $D_4$ acting on the four corners there is a single orbit of size $4$, and the stabiliser of corner $1$ is $\{e, s\}$, of size $2$. Note that $4 \cdot 2 = 8 = |D_4|$. This is no accident.

blocks.title: Orbit–stabiliser theorem
blocks.body:
If a finite group $G$ acts on a set $X$, then for every $x \in X$

$$|\operatorname{Orb}(x)| \cdot |\operatorname{Stab}(x)| = |G|.$$

Write $S = \operatorname{Stab}(x)$. For $g, h \in G$,

$$g\cdot x = h\cdot x \iff (h^{-1}g)\cdot x = x \iff h^{-1}g \in S \iff g \in hS \iff gS = hS.$$

(For the first step apply $h^{-1}$ to both sides, or $h$ to go back; the last step uses fact 3 of the proof of Lagrange, because $g \in gS \cap hS$.) Hence the rule $g\cdot x \mapsto gS$ is a well-defined, one-to-one correspondence between the points of the orbit and the left cosets of $S$. There are $|G|/|S|$ cosets by Lagrange, so $|\operatorname{Orb}(x)| = |G|/|S|$.

blocks.title: Burnside's lemma
blocks.body:
If a finite group $G$ acts on a finite set $X$, the number of orbits is

$$\#\text{orbits} = \frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}|\operatorname{Fix}(g)|.$$

In words: the number of essentially different objects is the average number of objects fixed by a symmetry. (The formula was known to Cauchy and Frobenius before Burnside, and is also called the Cauchy–Frobenius lemma.)

Count the pairs $(g, x) \in G \times X$ with $g\cdot x = x$ in two ways. Grouping by $g$, the count is $\sum_{g} |\operatorname{Fix}(g)|$. Grouping by $x$, it is $\sum_{x} |\operatorname{Stab}(x)|$, which by orbit–stabiliser equals $\sum_{x} |G|/|\operatorname{Orb}(x)|$.

Now split this last sum by orbits. An orbit $O$ contributes $\sum_{x \in O} |G|/|O| = |G|$. So the total is $|G|$ times the number of orbits, and dividing by $|G|$ gives the formula.
blocks.title: Proof of Burnside's lemma
How Burnside is used for colourings
blocks.body:
Suppose the positions of an object (corners, beads, faces) are coloured with $k$ colours, and a symmetry group $G$ permutes the positions. Two colourings count as the same if a symmetry carries one to the other, so the essentially different colourings are the orbits of $G$ acting on the $k^{\text{positions}}$ colourings.

Write a symmetry $g$ as a product of disjoint cycles on the positions. A colouring is fixed by $g$ exactly when it is constant along each cycle, so

$$|\operatorname{Fix}(g)| = k^{c(g)},$$

where $c(g)$ is the number of cycles of $g$, fixed positions counting as cycles of length one. Elements of the same geometric type (for example, all rotations by $120^\circ$ about a long diagonal of a cube) have the same $c(g)$, so in practice one makes a short table of types, how many elements of each type there are, and their cycle counts.
Find the order of every element of $(\mathbb Z/7)^\times = \{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ and check that each order divides $6$. Is the group generated by a single element?
blocks.solution:
List powers until $1$ appears.

- $1$: order $1$.
- $2$: $2, 4, 8 \equiv 1$, order $3$.
- $3$: $3, 9\equiv 2, 6, 18 \equiv 4, 12 \equiv 5, 15 \equiv 1$, order $6$.
- $4$: $4, 16\equiv 2, 8 \equiv 1$, order $3$.
- $5$: $5, 25 \equiv 4, 20 \equiv 6, 30 \equiv 2, 10 \equiv 3, 15 \equiv 1$, order $6$.
- $6$: $6, 36 \equiv 1$, order $2$.

The orders $1, 3, 6, 3, 6, 2$ all divide $|G| = 6$, as Lagrange requires. Since $3$ has order $6$, its powers exhaust the group, so the group is cyclic, generated by $3$ (and also by $5$). In the language of [[order-primroot]], $3$ and $5$ are the primitive roots modulo $7$. The subgroups are $\{1\}$, $\{1,6\}$, $\{1,2,4\}$ and the whole group, of orders $1, 2, 3, 6$.
blocks.title: Orders in the group modulo 7

blocks.body: Let $G$ be a group in which $g^2 = e$ for every element $g$. Prove that $G$ is abelian.
blocks.solution:
The condition $g^2 = e$ says $g = g^{-1}$ for every $g$. Take any $a, b \in G$. Applying this to $ab$, then the rule for the inverse of a product, then the condition to $a$ and $b$:

$$ab = (ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1} = ba.$$

So any two elements commute. (Example: $\mathbb Z/2 \times \mathbb Z/2$, the group of symmetries of a non-square rectangle.)
blocks.title: Squares to the identity

blocks.body: Each corner of a square is painted one of $3$ colours. How many essentially different colourings are there if two colourings are the same when (a) a rotation carries one to the other, (b) any symmetry of the square, rotation or reflection, carries one to the other?
blocks.solution:
There are $3^4 = 81$ colourings. Use $|\operatorname{Fix}(g)| = 3^{c(g)}$.

(a) The rotation group has $4$ elements. The identity has $4$ cycles (fixes $81$ colourings); the rotations by $90^\circ$ and $270^\circ$ are single $4$-cycles ($3$ each); the rotation by $180^\circ$ is $(1\,3)(2\,4)$, two cycles ($9$). Burnside gives

$$\frac{81 + 3 + 9 + 3}{4} = \frac{96}{4} = 24.$$

(b) Add the four reflections. A diagonal reflection fixes two corners and swaps the other two: $3$ cycles, $27$ colourings each. A reflection through edge midpoints consists of two $2$-cycles: $9$ each. Now

$$\frac{96 + 27 + 27 + 9 + 9}{8} = \frac{168}{8} = 21.$$

The difference tells us something too. Each $D_4$-orbit is either a single rotation orbit (when a colouring can be rotated into its own mirror image) or the union of two rotation orbits (a mirror-image pair). If $m$ of the $21$ orbits split in two, then counting rotation orbits gives $24 = 21 + m$, so $m = 3$: there are exactly $3$ chiral pairs, that is, $3$ pairs of rotation classes that only a reflection can match up.

blocks.body: Each face of a cube is painted one of $3$ colours. How many colourings are there up to rotation of the cube? Find also the general formula for $k$ colours.

blocks.body:
- The converse of Lagrange is false. The group $A_4$ of even permutations of four objects (equivalently, the rotations of a regular tetrahedron) has order $12$ but no subgroup of order $6$.
- Composition conventions differ between books: some write $rs$ for "first $r$, then $s$". Since groups need not be abelian, check the convention before multiplying.
- In Burnside's lemma the average is over group elements, not over types of elements. Each type must be weighted by how many elements it contains (in the cube, $8$ rotations of the $120^\circ$ type, not $1$).
- A subset whose size divides $|G|$ need not be a subgroup; closure and inverses must be checked. Likewise, a set with an operation is not a group until closure is verified, as the example of multiplication modulo $6$ shows.
- Orbit–stabiliser needs a genuine action: the symmetries must map the set $X$ into itself and satisfy $g\cdot(h\cdot x) = (gh)\cdot x$.

Lagrange's theorem is the abstract reason behind [[fermat-euler]], and the finer fact that $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$ is always cyclic is the subject of [[order-primroot]]. The next step in the theory is [[group-homomorphisms]]: maps that preserve the operation, normal subgroups, and quotient groups such as $\mathbb Z/n = \mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$. Actions are developed further in [[group-actions]] (the class equation and the Sylow theorems grow out of orbit–stabiliser).

Adding a second operation leads to [[rings]] and fields ([[finite-fields]], [[fields-ext]]), and [[galois]] theory attaches a group of symmetries to the roots of a polynomial. In physics, continuous groups of symmetries such as the rotation group and the unitary groups $SU(N)$ are the gauge groups of [[yang-mills]] theory.

1. Show that every group of even order contains an element of order $2$.
2. List all subgroups of $\mathbb Z/12$ and check that their orders divide $12$.
3. Prove that a group of prime order $p$ is cyclic, and that every element other than $e$ generates it.
4. Use Burnside's lemma to count necklaces of $6$ beads in $2$ colours, where two necklaces are the same if one is a rotation of the other.
